name: Orchids — 60 by habit and region
status: 5 archetypal species (full list archived in docs/plant_archive)
notes: Kew accepts ~28,000 orchid species, so this is a curated set: tropical epiphytes (moth, vanda, dendrobium, cattleya, bucket, Darwin's), cloud-forest miniatures (masdevallia, dracula), savanna and desert orchids, the northern bog and fen orchids, European chalk-grassland mimics (bee, fly, lizard), the leafless ones that live entirely on fungi (bird's-nest, coralroot, the European ghost orchid), Australian heath oddities, and the great cliff clumps. Rules they add: dust seed on the wind that germinates only where the right fungus already lives (reads the fungi ledger), and most need one specific pollinator — the orchid is the plant that tells you whether the food web is whole. Some blooms are weather-gated (pigeon orchid 9 days after a storm; sun orchid only in full sun).

ground.name: Pink lady's slipper

growth.juvenile_note: The dust-like seed needs a soil fungus: it swells into a tiny white protocorm that lives underground, feeding on the fungus, for one to several years before a first small pleated leaf appears. Young plants carry one, later two, broad, ribbed, hairy elliptic basal leaves lying close to the ground; only after many years does a leafless stalk lift the pink pouch flower.
growth.source: Wikipedia Cypripedium acaule (takes many years from seed to mature plant; two elliptic basal leaves; to 0.4 m; flowers Apr-Jun; deceptive, nectarless, bumblebee queens; partial shade, acid pine and oak woods; mycorrhizal pelotons); years to first leaf, flowering and lifespan estimated from Cypripedium demography literature (Gill, Primack)

ground.name: Bee orchid

growth.juvenile_note: Dust-like seed germinates only with a Tulasnella fungus, forming a tiny underground protocorm fed by the fungus for months to years. The first visible plant is a small rosette of 2-5 grey-green, oval-lance leaves that appears in autumn and grows slowly through winter; after several years a 20-40 cm stem rises in early summer with up to 12 flowers whose furry brown lip mimics a bee.
growth.source: Wikipedia Ophrys apifera (rosettes appear in autumn and grow through winter; flowers mid-April in S Europe, June-July in UK; 1-12 flowers; mostly self-pollinating in the north, Eucera bees in the Mediterranean; germination needs Tulasnella and may take months or years underground); Wells & Cox population studies (short-lived, often flowers once or twice)

epiphyte.name: Moth orchid
epiphyte.origin: Malesia to New Guinea and Australia

growth.juvenile_note: Dust-like seeds germinate only with a mycorrhizal fungus, swelling into a tiny green protocorm a few mm across with fine hairs; the first strap leaf and silvery-green roots follow after months. Young plants are a pair of small, fleshy, broad oval leaves on a very short stem, gripping bark with thick flat roots and adding 1-2 leaves a year.
growth.source: Estimated from Phalaenopsis seed-culture practice (protocorms in weeks, first leaf in 2-3 months, flowering size about 3-4 years from sowing) and the species' ecology as a shade-loving lowland epiphyte; lifespan estimated

epiphyte.name: Ghost orchid

growth.juvenile_note: Dust-like seed germinates only with a specific fungus into a tiny protocorm on the bark of pond apple or pop ash. The plant never makes real leaves: the young orchid is a few flat, grey-green photosynthetic roots radiating from a minute stem, slowly spreading into a flat root web 18-20 cm across before it can flower.
growth.source: Wikipedia Dendrophylax lindenii (leafless, leaves reduced to scales; flowers only once the root mass is ~180-200 mm across; flowers Jun-Aug, white, 3-4 x 7-9 cm; hawkmoth-pollinated; on Annona glabra and Fraxinus caroliniana in swamp forest; seedlings very hard to raise). Years to flowering and lifespan estimated.

epiphyte.name: Leopard orchid

growth.juvenile_note: Starts as a dust-like seed that must meet a fungus; it swells into a tiny green protocorm on bark, then a thread of roots and one or two narrow strap leaves. Over years it builds a clump of upright, yellow, cane-like pseudobulbs (to 60 cm) with 6-7 pleated strap leaves near the top, ringed by a basket of stiff, upward-pointing white aerial roots that trap leaf litter.
growth.source: Wikipedia (Ansellia africana: robust clumps, some estimated over a tonne; yellow cane-like pseudobulbs to 60 cm with 6-7 leathery plicate leaves; upward-pointing white aerial roots forming a litter basket; panicles to 85 cm with 10-100 fragrant flowers 6 cm across, each lasting up to ~10 days). Germination, growth and ages estimated from orchid biology.
